items.question: Where does the extra warmth in a warm-up come from?
options: Blood carrying heat out of your core
Friction between the bones in a joint
Muscles making heat as they work
Warmer air reaching the skin
items.explanation: Working muscle is a bit wasteful: a lot of the energy it uses leaves as heat rather than movement. That is why you can warm up on a cold morning without the air changing at all.

items.question: What does hot weather change about warming up?
options: Nothing, you warm up the same way
It can be shorter, not skipped
It removes the need for one
It should be longer than usual
items.explanation: Heat loosens skin and surface muscle quickly, but a warm-up is also rehearsal: it is where your body works out the movement before the effort counts. That part does not come free with the weather.

items.question: What separates feeling stiff from feeling sore?
options: Stiffness eases as you move around
Stiffness only happens in the morning
Soreness is always worse than stiffness
They tend to arrive at the same time
items.explanation: Stiffness is about how a joint feels when it has been still; soreness is about how a muscle feels when you press or load it. Stiffness usually improves within a few minutes of moving. Soreness takes days and does not care that you have got going.

items.question: You have ten minutes in total. How does a warm-up fit in?
options: Skip it and use all ten on the work
Stretch on the floor for five minutes
Walk briskly for eight of them
Start with an easier version of it
items.explanation: A warm-up does not have to be a separate activity that eats your ten minutes. The first easy round of the thing you are about to do is a warm-up, and it costs you almost no time at all.

items.question: What is your body doing in the first couple of minutes of effort?
options: Shifting breathing and blood flow up
Using up the last of yesterday's energy
Waiting for the muscles to unfreeze
Working at its hardest point of the day
items.explanation: Your muscles ask for more oxygen the instant you start, but breathing and circulation take a minute or two to catch up. That gap is why minute two often feels worse than minute ten, even though you are going the same speed.

items.question: You warm up, then sit and talk for twenty minutes. What happened to it?
options: It stays with you for about an hour
It counts as your cool-down instead
It fades, so ease back in again
It works better after a rest
items.explanation: The warmth and the blood flow drain away faster than people expect. You do not need the whole warm-up again, but the first minute back should look like a beginning, not a continuation.

items.question: Someone returns to a routine after three weeks off. What does soreness do?
options: It is gone for good after the first time
It comes back, though usually less
It is worse than the very first session
It returns only if the routine changed
items.explanation: Whatever your body learned the first time around does not vanish in three weeks, but it does fade. Expect an echo of the original soreness rather than a repeat of it, and it is not a sign the time off undid everything.

items.question: What does a gentle seated routine need before it starts?
options: Nothing, it is gentle already
A full stretch of every muscle
Five minutes of brisk walking
A few smaller, slower moves
items.explanation: A warm-up scales to the thing it is warming up for. For a seated routine that means the same movements through a smaller range first, which is also how you find out what your body is offering today.

items.question: You are sore in a muscle you did not know you had. What does that mean?
options: You used it in an unfamiliar way
You injured something small there
That muscle was weak to begin with
You did the movement incorrectly
items.explanation: Most muscles go unnoticed because nothing has ever asked them to work in that direction. A new movement finds them, and the soreness is really just an introduction.

items.question: Two people do the same new workout. One is sore after, one is not. What does that show?
options: The sore one worked much harder
One of them warmed up better
Mostly how new it was to each
Their ages must be different
items.explanation: Soreness tracks unfamiliarity far more than it tracks effort, and people differ a lot in how much they get from the same work. It is a poor way to compare two people and a poor way to grade yourself.

items.question: What matters most when picking shoes to walk in?
options: That they match your arch type
That they fit and you can move
That they have the most cushion
That they are under a year old
items.explanation: Arch-matching charts and replacement schedules sell a lot of shoes, and the evidence behind them is thin. Shoes that fit, stay on, and let your foot bend cover most of what actually matters.

items.question: You are learning a new movement and want to know if you have it right. What helps most?
options: Go by how the movement feels
Count how many you can do
Watch the video one more time
Record it and watch it back
items.explanation: When a movement is new, the feel of it is the least reliable thing about it: your sense of where your limbs are has not caught up yet. Seeing yourself from outside closes that gap in one go.

items.question: Which trip hazard at home is the easiest one to miss?
options: A rug with a curled edge
A steep flight of stairs
A wet bathroom floor
A high step at the door
items.explanation: The dramatic hazards get handled, because they look like hazards. A flat rug edge sits at ankle height, matches the floor, and has been there so long that nobody sees it any more.

items.question: A watch shows a heart rate above the 'maximum' for your age. What is the sensible read?
options: You went past a safe ceiling
A high number means you are fit
Those numbers are rough guesses
Your heart is working too hard
items.explanation: The age formula is an average with a wide spread around it, so plenty of ordinary people sit above their own number. Wrist readings also jump. How you actually feel is the better instrument.

items.question: Why is it easy to end up short of water on a cold day?
options: Cold water is harder to absorb
Cold makes you feel less thirsty
The body stores less in the cold
You sweat the same as in summer
items.explanation: Cold blunts thirst, and you are also losing water with every breath you can see in front of you. Nothing about the day feels like a hot one, so nobody thinks to drink.

items.question: Your form gets sloppy on the last few reps. What is that a sign of?
options: A warm-up that was far too short
A movement too advanced for now
The point where the gains happen
The muscle is out of steam
items.explanation: Quality falling off is the clearest signal a muscle gives that it is done. Stopping there costs you almost nothing, because the messy reps were never the ones doing the work.

items.question: Why do people who feel steady still use the handrail on stairs?
options: It takes some weight off the knees
It is there for the unplanned slip
It keeps you walking more slowly
It stops your arms from swinging
items.explanation: A handrail is not support for people who need support. It is a thing to catch that you do not have to think about, and you only find out you needed it after you already needed it.

items.question: You need a chair to hold for a standing exercise. Which chair is the wrong one?
options: One with arms
One with no cushion
One on wheels
One with a tall back
items.explanation: A rolling chair moves at exactly the moment you want something not to. Cushions, arms and back height change nothing about whether it holds still, which is the only job you are giving it.

items.question: A child wants to lift something heavy. What matters more than the weight?
options: Whether they can control it
Whether they are tall enough
How many times they lift it
Whether their back stays straight
items.explanation: Can they pick it up, carry it and set it down without it getting away from them? A load under control is a load their body can learn from. One that is steering them is the one that causes trouble.

items.question: What happens as a walking route becomes very familiar?
options: Your stride gets shorter over time
You notice more of the details
Your pace stops changing at all
Attention drops on familiar ground
items.explanation: Walking a known route hands the job to autopilot, which is efficient and slightly careless. The curb that has been there for years is exactly the one nobody looks at any more.

items.question: What does slowing a movement down do to it?
options: Makes it easier on the muscle
Makes the muscle work longer
Makes it safer but pointless
Makes it mostly a stretch
items.explanation: The muscle is under load for the whole time you are moving, so taking four seconds instead of one roughly quadruples that. It is the simplest way to make a movement harder when you have nothing to add to it.

items.question: What does using a movement's full range add?
options: Strength across more positions
A faster set, with less effort
Less work for the muscle overall
More reps before you get tired
items.explanation: Muscles get stronger mostly in the positions you train them in. Cutting a movement short builds strength in the middle of the range and leaves the ends, which are the positions real life keeps putting you in.

items.question: Can strength work make you more flexible?
options: No, it always tightens muscles
Only stretching changes range
Yes, full-range work does it
Yes, if you also hold stretches
items.explanation: A muscle loaded through its whole range is being asked to produce force in a long position, which is most of what a stretch asks for too. The old idea that lifting makes you stiff came from watching people train through half a range.

items.question: Why is one arm usually a little stronger than the other?
options: It has more muscle fibers
Blood reaches it more easily
Its bones are slightly longer
It gets more use day to day
items.explanation: You open doors, carry bags and throw with one side without deciding to, and that adds up to years of extra practice. Which is also why the gap narrows once the quieter side gets its own turn.

items.question: What is the rest between sets for?
options: Letting the soreness settle down
Letting the muscle refuel a bit
Giving the muscle time to grow
Cooling the muscle back down
items.explanation: Muscles run the first part of a hard set on a fast-burning fuel they keep on site, and it takes a minute or two to restock. Rest too little and the next set is limited by fuel rather than by strength.

items.question: How many days a week of muscle-strengthening activity do U.S. guidelines suggest for adults?
options: At least two
At least five
Every day
About one
items.explanation: The guideline says at least two days, and it is a floor rather than a target. It also does not say what kind: carrying, climbing and bodyweight movements all count as strengthening.

items.question: One arm is in a cast. What does training the other arm do for it?
options: It speeds up the healing
It makes the gap wider
It keeps some strength there
It tires the resting arm out
items.explanation: Strength is partly a skill held in the nervous system, and that part is not fully one-sided. The resting limb keeps more than it would have if nothing was being trained at all.

items.question: Two people do the same stretches for months, and only one can touch their toes. Why?
options: One stretches longer each time
Hamstring strength differs a lot
Only one bothered to warm up
Their proportions differ a lot
items.explanation: How far your fingers get depends on the length of your arms, legs and back and the shape of your hip sockets, none of which a routine changes. Compare your own reach over time; comparing it to somebody else's tells you almost nothing.

items.question: Why does holding a plank get harder when nothing is moving?
options: Muscle fibers tire and hand over
The muscle slowly stretches out
Your bones take more of the load
Breathing gets harder over time
items.explanation: In a hold, your fibers take turns rather than all pulling at once. As the rested ones run out, the same position needs more of what is left, which is why second forty-five feels nothing like second five.

items.question: Why do strength gains slow down after the first couple of months?
options: The muscle has reached its limit
The exercises get stale to you
The easiest changes come first
You stop trying as hard by then
items.explanation: Early on your body is learning the movement, which is quick. After that it has to actually build, which is slow. The slowdown is a change of gear, not a sign anything went wrong.
